intro:
Chapter 26 treats Tokio, Rayon, Crossbeam, and the futures combinators as complementary executors rather than interchangeable concurrency libraries, and these exercises make you commit to the matching every time. The decision order is always the same: first ask whether the dominant cost is waiting or computing, then ask whether the unit you own is a runtime-spawned task, a locally driven future, a thread-pool job, or a channel message. Get that mapping right and the rest is configuration; get it wrong and you put CPU-heavy work on async workers or force a waiting-oriented runtime to schedule dense compute.

The exercises build from classification toward operable design. You sort four workloads onto their primary tool, find CPU-bound work stranded on Tokio workers, implement a bounded worker queue where admission is an explicit policy, repair an async pipeline so cancellation and retry live in one orchestration shell, and finally design pool routing and a public task API that another team can run safely. The lab grounds all of it in one runnable program: a bounded Crossbeam channel feeding a worker that counts accepted jobs, counts one retryable job separately, and observes an explicit shutdown signal when the channel closes.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose Tokio, Rayon, Crossbeam, or futures utilities from the workload
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Apply the chapter's decision order to each case: first name the dominant cost (waiting or CPU), then name the unit of work (a spawned runtime task, a local future, a pool job, or a channel message). The four workloads sort cleanly because each one is built around a different unit.

The TCP accept loop with many idle sockets is waiting-dominated. Almost every socket is parked waiting for bytes, and the runtime makes progress on whichever one becomes ready. This is the canonical Tokio case: each connection is a cheap spawned task that costs almost nothing while idle, and the runtime multiplexes thousands of them onto a few worker threads. Threads-per-connection would waste stacks on sockets that are doing nothing.

The large batch scoring pass over numeric data is CPU-dominated, and the unit is one data set you want to saturate cores with. This is Rayon. A par_iter splits the data across a work-stealing pool and rejoins the result with no manual thread choreography, and crucially it does not borrow an async runtime to do dense arithmetic. Putting this on Tokio workers would monopolize them and starve any concurrent IO.

The thread-based pipeline with bounded handoff between worker stages is coordination-dominated: the unit is a message crossing a queue between OS threads. This is Crossbeam. A crossbeam::channel::bounded gives you the bounded handoff directly, ownership moves with each message, and the bound is the backpressure between stages. You are not waiting on IO here and you are not saturating one data set; you are coordinating threads, which is exactly Crossbeam's model.

The local set of futures you want to poll as they complete without spawning each one is the FuturesUnordered case, because the futures themselves are the unit of composition. You already hold the futures and only need to drive them together inside one task; spawning each one would hand them to the runtime as independent tasks you do not want. FuturesUnordered keeps them local and yields each result as it finishes. The key distinction the chapter draws is spawned tasks (JoinSet, runtime-owned, progress even when you are not awaiting the set) versus locally composed futures (FuturesUnordered, driven only while you poll the set).
criteria: Each workload is assigned to one primary tool and justified by scheduling shape: accept loop to Tokio (waiting), batch scoring to Rayon (CPU saturation), thread pipeline to Crossbeam (coordination), local futures to FuturesUnordered (composition unit).
Spawned tasks are distinguished from locally composed futures: JoinSet hands work to the runtime, FuturesUnordered keeps futures inside the current task.
IO-bound (accept loop) and CPU-bound (batch scoring) workloads are kept on separate tools rather than collapsed onto one library.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find CPU-bound work left on Tokio workers
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Walk the handler step by step and label each step by whether it parks the worker or pins it. Reading from the socket is a natural async wait: the .await yields the worker while bytes are in flight, so it belongs on the runtime. The database call is the same shape, an async wait that releases the worker until the response returns. Publishing to a queue is typically another await, so it also stays. These steps are async-friendly precisely because they spend their time waiting, and a Tokio worker that is awaiting one connection is free to drive another.

The heavy checksum over the large parsed batch is the defect. It is computed inline in the async function, so it runs on a runtime worker thread and does not yield. While it runs, that worker cannot make progress on any other task. With a small worker pool, a few concurrent requests each computing a heavy checksum can pin every worker at once, and other connections that only need to be polled sit unserviced. This is runtime starvation: async did not make the CPU work parallel, it just put serial CPU work in the wrong place. The parse step sits on the boundary; if it is cheap it can stay, but if it is large it belongs with the checksum.

The fix depends on how much the batch stage dominates. If checksum computation is occasional relative to the IO, tokio::task::spawn_blocking is enough: move the owned parsed batch into the blocking closure so the heavy work runs on Tokio's separate blocking pool and the worker is freed to await the database call. The ownership transfer is what makes this clean, the closure takes the batch by value, so there is no borrow tangling the lifetimes across the await. If the batch stage is the real job of the service and runs on most requests, spawn_blocking is the wrong tool because the blocking pool is sized for occasional bridges, not steady dense compute; a dedicated Rayon pool is more honest, giving CPU work its own budget and work-stealing parallelism instead of overloading the blocking pool.

For observability, the signals are concrete. Runtime task scheduling latency (the delay between a task becoming ready and being polled) climbs when workers are pinned, so a rising poll latency or a Tokio worker that stays busy on compute confirms starvation. For the blocking path, watch the blocking-pool backlog or queue depth: if spawn_blocking jobs queue up because the pool is saturated, that is the signal you have outgrown spawn_blocking and need a real CPU pool.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Socket read, DB call, and publish stay async; the dominant cost there is waiting. The checksum moves to spawn_blocking (occasional) or a dedicated CPU pool (when the batch stage dominates).
criteria: Waiting-heavy steps (socket read, database call, publish) are separated from the CPU-heavy checksum step.
The checksum is moved to spawn_blocking via an owned-batch closure, with a stated reason (it pins a runtime worker), and a Rayon pool is named for the case where the batch stage dominates.
An observability hook is named: runtime scheduling/poll latency for starvation, and blocking-pool backlog or queue depth for blocking-pool overload.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement a bounded worker queue
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The point of this exercise is that a bounded queue is a policy decision, so the capacity must be visible in code rather than buried in a default. Construct the channel with an explicit capacity, here 2, using either tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(2) for an async service or crossbeam::channel::bounded(2) for a thread-based pipeline. The bound means a fast producer cannot grow memory without limit: once the queue is full, a send blocks (or awaits) until the worker drains an item, which is backpressure pushed back onto the producer instead of silent unbounded buffering.

Work crosses the boundary by ownership transfer, not by sharing mutable state. Each job is an owned value moved into the channel with send, and the worker takes ownership when it recv's. Because the queue owns admission, the producer does not need a broad shared lock to publish, the channel is the synchronization, and the only thing shared is the queue's own internal coordination. This is the chapter's contrast with sharing a mutable buffer behind a lock: here the data moves, so there is no aliasing to reason about and no lock contention on a shared structure.

Count the retryable item separately from accepted normal work so the two outcomes are distinguishable in the accounting, exactly as the orchestration shell in the chapter keeps retry bookkeeping in one place. A job tagged retry increments a retried counter; any other job increments accepted. Finally, add an explicit stop condition: closing the sender (dropping every tx) causes recv to return an error, the worker's loop exits, and the worker records that it observed the shutdown. Wiring the signal in this way once makes adding real mid-flight cancellation later a small change rather than a redesign.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Capacity is explicit at construction, jobs move by ownership through the bounded channel, retries are counted apart from accepted work, and dropping the sender is the visible stop condition.
criteria: The channel is constructed with an explicit bounded capacity, not an unbounded default, and the capacity value is visible in code.
Each job is an owned value moved through send/recv; no shared mutable buffer or broad lock is used to publish work.
Retried items are counted separately from accepted work, and the runnable lab prints capacity 2, accepted 2, retried 1, and cancelled true.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair async orchestration with cancellation and retry
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Two defects make this service hard to operate. First, there is no stop signal, so the spawned child tasks have no way to be told to wind down; the only way to stop is to kill the process, which abandons in-flight work. Second, retry is implemented by the task body recursively re-invoking itself on failure. That hides the retry budget inside each task, makes the depth uncapped (a job that always fails recurses forever), and scatters the retry accounting across every handler so no single place knows how many retries are outstanding. The chapter's rule is the opposite: retry budgeting and cancellation belong in one visible orchestration shell, not inside the task body.

For the stop signal, choose by shape. A watch channel is the right primitive when one shutdown flag must be observed by many tasks, because every task can hold a receiver and react to the same change; a oneshot fits a single consumer, and an abort handle (or JoinSet's abort_all) fits forced mid-flight cancellation. The clean design is admission plus draining as one control flow: a watch::channel(false) broadcasts shutdown, the producer stops accepting new work when it sees the flag, and the orchestrator then drains the tasks already in flight rather than dropping them. Stop admitting, then drain, is easier to reason about than abrupt abort.

Replace the recursive retry with a bounded policy in the orchestration shell. Keep the task body small, it just returns Ok(id) or Err(id), and let the shell own the retry counter and backoff. When a result comes back Err, the shell increments a retry counter, checks it against a budget, and only then re-submits the job; when the budget is exhausted it records a terminal failure. This caps retries, makes them observable from one place, and keeps each task trivial.

For centralizing completion, JoinSet is the better fit here because the unit you own is runtime-spawned tasks, and that matches the workload: an IO-heavy service where each job should make progress on the runtime independently. JoinSet::join_next yields results as tasks finish, so the shell can drain, inspect, and re-spawn retries in one loop. FuturesUnordered would be the choice only if you wanted to keep the futures local and drive them inside one task, which is not what a spawned-task service wants. This mirrors the chapter's Tokio orchestration example, where tasks live in a JoinSet that drains results while the bounded channel governs intake and the shutdown flag is observed in one place.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Retry budget and shutdown both live in the orchestration shell: a watch flag gates admission, the loop drains in-flight tasks, and JoinSet centralizes completion. The task body stays a one-liner.
criteria: Retry budgeting is moved out of recursive self-calls in the task body into a single bounded policy in the orchestration shell with an explicit RETRY_BUDGET cap.
An explicit cancellation path is added via a watch shutdown flag that stops admission and then drains in-flight tasks.
Spawned-task orchestration with JoinSet is chosen over FuturesUnordered, justified by an IO-heavy service whose unit is runtime-owned tasks.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose thread pools and backpressure for a mixed service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The pipeline accept -> parse -> enrich -> persist -> publish has three distinct work shapes, so it legitimately uses more than one executor. Accept and persist and publish are waiting-dominated (sockets and a datastore), so they stay on Tokio runtime workers, where idle connections cost almost nothing and the runtime multiplexes them. Parse is cheap structural work and can stay inline on the runtime if it is light. Enrich is the CPU-heavy stage, and the central design decision is that it must not run inline on runtime workers, because dense compute there pins the workers and starves the waiting-heavy front and back of the pipeline.

Give the enrich stage a real CPU boundary. Because enrichment is CPU-bound and bursty traffic means many items arrive at once, Rayon is a better fit than a large number of small spawn_blocking tasks: Rayon's work-stealing pool keeps cores saturated and rejoins results without the blocking pool filling up. A flood of small blocking tasks would overload Tokio's blocking pool, which is sized for occasional bridges, not steady compute. So the route is async accept/parse on the runtime, a handoff into a bounded queue feeding a dedicated Rayon pool for enrich, then back to the runtime for persist and publish.

Place backpressure deliberately, and put the budget on the expensive stage, not only the front door. The internal queue feeding enrichment should be bounded so a burst of accepted connections cannot pile up unbounded ahead of the slow CPU stage; when that queue fills, admission slows, which is the backpressure propagating to the accept loop. A concurrency cap (a semaphore) belongs in front of persist if the datastore has a connection limit, so in-flight writes stay within what the store tolerates. The chapter's guidance is explicit here: the budget should follow the expensive stage, so the enrichment intake queue and the persist concurrency cap are where the limits matter most.

For clean rolling shutdown, broadcast a shutdown signal (a watch flag), stop the accept loop from admitting new connections, then drain the bounded queue and let in-flight enrich and persist work finish before exit. Before calling the design production-ready, require at least these metrics: enrichment intake queue depth (rising depth means the CPU stage is the bottleneck), in-flight task count and Rayon pool utilization (to size the pool), blocking-pool backlog if any spawn_blocking remains, and shutdown latency (how long draining takes). Those four let an operator see which stage is saturated and whether shutdown drains cleanly.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A routing sketch: waiting stages on Tokio, enrich on a dedicated Rayon pool, a bounded queue before enrich and a semaphore before persist, with the budget placed on the expensive stage.
criteria: At least one bounded queue (before enrich) and one concurrency cap (semaphore before persist) are placed deliberately.
Enrichment is given a real CPU boundary on a dedicated Rayon pool rather than left inline on runtime workers, with Rayon preferred over many small blocking tasks.
At least two observability hooks are named: enrich intake queue depth, in-flight task count / Rayon utilization, blocking-pool backlog, and shutdown latency.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a task API another team can operate safely
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The guiding principle is that budgets and outcomes should be first-class in the API, not hidden constants, because another team has to operate this without reading the implementation. Start with ownership at the submission boundary. The submission API should own the work item: callers hand it a value by move (a Job, or a boxed closure plus its owned inputs) so the work can outlive the caller's stack frame and be scheduled freely. The alternative, a spawned-work API that borrows from caller-held data, drags lifetimes through the whole pipeline and forces 'static-or-scoped contortions on callers. The API may borrow caller data only locally during the submit call itself, for example to read configuration, but anything that crosses onto a worker must be owned. This is also what lets the same library run on Tokio for IO-heavy users and on a CPU pool for batch-heavy users: the owned job is portable across both backends.

Make at least one resource budget visible to callers or configuration. Expose queue capacity, a concurrency cap, and a retry budget as constructor or builder parameters (a PoolConfig with queue_capacity, max_in_flight, and retry_budget), with documented defaults rather than buried constants. Callers either set them explicitly or inherit the documented default, but in both cases the budget is discoverable. This follows the chapter's point that a task library is easier to operate when budgets are first-class.

Give callers a clear cancellation path and a structured outcome. For cancellation, return a handle from submit that supports an explicit cancel/abort, and define drop semantics clearly (dropping the handle either detaches or cancels, documented either way); a timeout wrapper can sit on top for time-bounded waits. For the result, return an enum that distinguishes the three real outcomes so a caller cannot confuse them: Outcome::Done(T) for success, Outcome::Retryable(E) for a failure the pipeline already exhausted its retry budget on, and Outcome::Cancelled for work stopped by signal or shutdown. A structured enum beats Result<T, E> here because cancellation is not the same as failure and callers need to branch on it.

Finally, name one testing hook and one observability hook. For testing, make the backend injectable: a trait-object or generic executor so tests can run the same submission API against a deterministic in-line executor instead of a real runtime, making retry and cancellation paths testable without timing flakiness. For observability, expose queue depth and in-flight count (and a shutdown-drain metric) through a metrics handle, so operators can see saturation and confirm clean shutdown.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Owned Job at the boundary, budgets in PoolConfig, a structured Outcome enum, a JobHandle for cancellation, an injectable Pool trait for testing, and a metrics hook for operators.
criteria: The submission boundary owns the Job by move rather than borrowing caller data, avoiding a lifetime-heavy spawned-work API while staying portable across Tokio and CPU-pool backends.
At least one resource budget (queue_capacity, max_in_flight, retry_budget) is made visible via PoolConfig with documented defaults.
Callers get an explicit cancellation path (JobHandle::cancel plus documented drop semantics) and a structured Outcome enum distinguishing Done, Retryable, and Cancelled.
A testing hook (injectable Pool trait for a deterministic executor) and an observability hook (PoolMetrics queue depth and in-flight count) are named.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab fixes three defects in the starter. The starter wrote retried += 0, which never counts the retry, and it left cancelled initialized to false and never set; it also did not tie the shutdown observation to the queue closing. The solution corrects the retry increment to retried += 1, sets cancelled = true after the loop ends, and uses the drop of the sender as the explicit stop condition.

The flow is straightforward. The bounded channel is built with an explicit capacity of 2, so the queue's admission policy is visible in code and a fast producer cannot buffer without limit. Three owned jobs move across the boundary: "parse" and "flush" are normal work and each increment accepted (giving 2), while "retry" is counted separately and increments retried (giving 1). Work crosses by ownership transfer through send/recv, so no shared mutable buffer or lock is involved.

When the producer calls drop(tx), every sender is gone, so rx.recv() returns Err, the while loop exits, and the worker sets cancelled = true to record that it observed the shutdown signal. The thread is joined, its tuple is returned, and the four println! calls emit capacity = 2, accepted = 2, retried = 1, and cancelled = true, which is exactly the expected output. Wiring the stop signal in this way once makes adding real mid-flight cancellation, with select! and an abort path, a small later change rather than a redesign.

reviewAnswers.question: What practical signal tells you a workload wants Tokio instead of Rayon?
reviewAnswers.answer: The deciding signal is that the dominant cost is waiting rather than computing: the work spends most of its time parked on IO (sockets, datastores, timers) with many units idle at once. Tokio multiplexes those waiting units onto a few worker threads cheaply, so thousands of mostly-idle connections cost almost nothing. Rayon is the opposite case, where the job is to saturate cores over a data set; if your work would keep a CPU busy rather than parked, that is the Rayon signal, and putting it on Tokio workers would only pin them and starve the IO.

reviewAnswers.question: When is FuturesUnordered calmer than JoinSet, and when is the reverse true?
reviewAnswers.answer: FuturesUnordered is calmer when you already hold a set of futures and only need to drive them together inside the current task, because it keeps everything local: nothing crosses a task boundary, the futures advance only while you poll the set, and there is no per-task spawn overhead. JoinSet is the calmer choice when the unit you actually own is runtime-spawned tasks, because each future is handed to the runtime as an independent task that makes progress on worker threads even when you are not awaiting the set, and join_next drains completions for you. So the rule is FuturesUnordered for local composition of futures you already have, JoinSet when you want the runtime to own and schedule each unit independently.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a bounded queue already an API and overload decision, not only an implementation detail?
reviewAnswers.answer: A bound is a policy: it sets the maximum amount of in-flight work the stage will admit, and when it is full it forces backpressure onto the producer instead of silently buffering. That choice determines how the system behaves under overload, whether a fast producer can exhaust memory, whether latency degrades gracefully or the service falls over, so it is visible behavior callers and operators depend on, not a hidden constant. Because it governs admission and overload response, the capacity belongs in the API surface or configuration where it can be seen and tuned, not buried in an unbounded default.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the difference between cancellation as task drop, cancellation as explicit signal, and retry as policy?
reviewAnswers.answer: Cancellation as task drop means stopping work by dropping the future or aborting the task: the work simply stops at its next yield point, which is abrupt and may leave partial state, so it suits forced mid-flight termination. Cancellation as an explicit signal is cooperative: a watch flag or oneshot tells tasks to wind down, so the orchestrator can stop admitting new work and drain in-flight work cleanly, which is easier to reason about and to test. Retry as policy is a separate concern entirely; it is the bounded budget and backoff that decide whether failed work is re-submitted, and the chapter's point is that it belongs in one orchestration shell with an explicit cap rather than hidden as recursion inside the task body.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should CPU-heavy work have its own budget even inside an async service?
reviewAnswers.answer: Async makes IO concurrent, but it does not make CPU work parallel or non-blocking; a heavy compute step run inline on a runtime worker pins that worker and prevents it from polling any other task, so a few such steps can starve the whole runtime. Giving CPU work its own budget, a spawn_blocking allowance for occasional bridges or a dedicated Rayon pool when compute dominates, keeps the runtime workers free to service waiting work and keeps latency predictable. The budget should follow the expensive stage, so the CPU lane is sized and bounded on its own rather than competing with the IO front door for the same worker threads.
